title: Community Partnership that Can Influence a Decision
audience: Staff developing services, policy, learning, or community relationships; supervisors and managers examining the actual influence, resources, and responsibility in participation.

slides.text:
One DSD People, Access and Culture
Community Partnership that Can Influence a Decision
Connect community knowledge with open choices, usable participation, and a truthful account of its influence.
Advanced self-directed learning
slides.narration: An invitation can be sincere and still leave people with little influence over the question that matters to them. This course examines what participation can actually change. Through fictional DSD service and workplace examples, you will compare open choices, practical burdens, and different accounts of how input was used. The purpose is a relationship grounded in clear expectations and useful knowledge, while preserving actual agency responsibilities and avoiding promises that an invitation cannot fulfill.

slides.text:
A finished design, an open invitation
Staff invite people to “co-design” a service introduction. The service route and explanation are already settled; only the photograph can change.

What influence does this offer? A useful invitation can be limited, but its description should match the choice that remains open.
slides.narration: The problem is not that every invitation must reopen every decision. A settled decision may need a good explanation, and a limited design question can still benefit from input. The difficulty comes when the invitation promises more than people can influence. Consider how that gap may affect someone deciding whether to contribute their time and knowledge. If repeated, it can make later invitations less credible and leave the organization hearing mainly from those already comfortable with its approach.

slides.text:
Participation has a specific purpose
Informing, asking for advice, and developing an approach together offer different kinds of influence.

Describe the question, what can change, and the actual decision responsibility. Do not call a reaction to a settled choice shared design.
slides.narration: The participation method should fit the purpose of the exchange. Asking for advice can reveal a concern about two workable options. Shared design can include examination of the problem and alternatives before they are fixed. Providing information about a completed decision is also legitimate when described accurately. These differences help a person understand what their contribution could accomplish. Actual agency authority remains relevant, and clarity about it can support a meaningful relationship rather than diminish the value of community knowledge.

slides.text:
Worked example: two invitations
A: “Help design our finished service.” No open choice is named.

B: “Examine the proposed question route. Its wording and contact options can change; the eligibility rule is outside this discussion.”

B offers a clearer contribution. Its practical arrangements and actual influence still need confirmation.
slides.narration: Invitation B gives the person a question they can consider before deciding to participate. It explains both an opening and a boundary. That does not make the invitation complete or establish a successful partnership. The person still needs to know how to contribute, how suggestions will be considered, and whether the arrangement is usable. The important comparison is between a vague promise of influence and a specific opportunity that can be examined. Honesty about a boundary leaves room for genuine contribution within it.

slides.text:
The finished service introduction
A fictional team calls its meeting co-design, but the service route and wording are settled. Participants can choose a photograph. What would make the invitation more honest?
A. Describe the actual choice and its limits, or reopen a relevant question through the responsible roles before promising shared design.
B. Keep the broad promise because it may attract more participants.
C. Give this meeting authority over every service rule.
In Slide Show view, select a response to explore its effects.
slides.narration: The invitation promises a wider contribution than the meeting offers. Choosing a photograph may be a legitimate limited question, but it is different from shaping a service route or its explanation. Your response should make that difference clear. A genuine opening could be sought through the actual responsibilities, or the invitation could describe the existing choice accurately. Repeated inflated invitations may reduce willingness to participate when more substantial input is needed later. The fictional case does not establish that participants agree, that a new opening will be granted, or that a changed design will improve service.

links.name: Answer 1
links.text: A. Describe the actual choice and its limits, or reopen a relevant question through the responsible roles before promising shared design.

links.name: Answer 2
links.text: B. Keep the broad promise because it may attract more participants.

links.name: Answer 3
links.text: C. Give this meeting authority over every service rule.

slides.text:
Why this response helps
This aligns the invitation with actual influence. Repeated inflated promises can narrow future participation. Describe the real choice or seek a genuine opening; neither action establishes agreement or a better service result.

Which part of this decision could a participant’s knowledge actually change?
Continue learning
Try another response
slides.narration: The response preserves honest participation without requiring every decision to reopen. It recognizes the limited choice and leaves a route to seek a more substantive opening through actual responsibilities. If vague promises repeat, useful knowledge may stop reaching the work. Clearer influence can help, but it does not establish participant agreement, available resources, or the effects of a future service change.

slides.text:
Consider the possible effects
A broad promise may bring people to a choice they cannot influence. Repetition can weaken future willingness to contribute. State the actual opening and limits; attendance does not establish endorsement.

Which part of this decision could a participant’s knowledge actually change?
Try another response
Continue learning
slides.narration: Attracting people through a promise they cannot fulfill may consume their effort without allowing the expected influence. Repetition can make later invitations less credible and privilege those already comfortable with the arrangement. A better invitation describes the real question and boundaries. The case does not show how participants would respond or establish that anyone has endorsed the finished service.

slides.text:
Consider the possible effects
An invitation cannot create authority over every rule. That promise can obscure real responsibilities and choices. Clarify the available influence and seek appropriate openings; no new decision power is established here.

Which part of this decision could a participant’s knowledge actually change?
Try another response
Continue learning
slides.narration: Shared design does not mean that a single meeting acquires every agency authority. That claim would be as misleading as the original invitation. Explain the actual responsibility and what remains open, and seek appropriate changes where needed. Meaningful input can inform decisions without making every participant responsible for every rule. No transfer of authority is supplied by this exercise.

slides.text:
Who helped define the problem?
A service question framed only around administrative speed may overlook understanding, usable support, or the burden of repeated contact.

Invite affected perspectives while the problem can still be examined. Their knowledge may change the question as well as the preferred answer.
slides.narration: Imagine a service review asking how to reduce telephone calls. A participant may explain that repeated calls occur because the notice does not answer a consequential question. That contribution changes what the team needs to examine. Reducing calls alone could make the problem harder to see. Community knowledge does not automatically establish the cause or determine the solution, but it can reveal a missing condition. An open problem discussion allows that knowledge to inform the actual comparison of options.

slides.text:
Make the decision role visible
Explain who considers contributions, what responsibilities remain, and how reasons can be communicated.

Welcoming people does not create identical authority. Meaningful influence can coexist with agency responsibilities when the available choice and consideration are clear.
slides.narration: A participant may reasonably ask who will decide what changes. Answering that question does not undermine collaboration; it makes the relationship more understandable. Avoid promising an authority that the exchange does not have. At the same time, existing authority is not evidence that a contribution has been considered. The useful account explains how the concern reached the choice and what reason supported the response. That distinction protects both the integrity of the agency responsibility and the substance of the partnership.

slides.text:
Practical conditions shape whose input arrives
Consider usable materials, communication support, preparation, timing, and the effort needed to contribute.

An open invitation is not the same as an available opportunity. Examine barriers without assuming that absent people lack interest or share one preference.
slides.narration: The invitation may be available to everyone while the practical route works for only some. A person may need accessible material, a different contribution method, or time to consider what the question means. These conditions can shape which perspectives enter the decision. Repetition can make a narrow participation route appear to produce a natural consensus. Ask about the actual barriers and varied preferences. Do not infer them solely from an identity, and do not interpret an absent contribution as agreement.

slides.text:
Expertise and the cost of contributing
Community expertise can require preparation, review, travel, or other effort. Examine how that effort is supported through actual approved arrangements.

Do not promise compensation or invent a rate. Make resource questions visible before asking people to provide substantial work.
slides.narration: A request for a quick reaction and a request to review a detailed proposal place different demands on a person. Naming the effort helps the appropriate colleagues consider what support is possible and how it would work within actual rules. The course does not authorize payment or establish a compensation scheme. Its point is that contribution has a cost even when no invoice appears. Repeated reliance on unsupported expertise can narrow participation to people and organizations with enough resources to absorb that cost.

slides.text:
Compare whole participation arrangements
Compare what is open, the material supplied, the contribution route, and how a response returns to participants.

Changing only the invitation may leave the same practical limits. A stronger alternative addresses the condition that keeps useful knowledge from entering the decision.
slides.narration: A more welcoming sentence may help, but it cannot supply an unavailable document or create room for a concern after the decision is fixed. Compare the complete arrangements. One might invite comments on a finished draft, while another offers an understandable draft and a specific question before a relevant choice closes. Each has different demands and influence. A useful comparison recognizes those differences without declaring one method universally best. The right inquiry is what arrangement fits the actual question and people involved.

slides.text:
Onboarding input after the choice closes
New staff explain that onboarding omitted a usable question route. The next version is already final. How can their knowledge still be treated seriously?
A. Announce that the new staff approved the finished version.
B. Explain what can happen next, preserve the concern, and connect it to an appropriate future opening without promising a change.
C. Discard the concern because it arrived after this version closed.
In Slide Show view, select a response to explore its effects.
slides.narration: The staff account identifies a condition in onboarding, and the closed version defines a current limit. Both can be true. A respectful response explains whether the concern can inform another appropriate question or a future revision, without pretending that the finished version has already changed. If the missing question route recurs, it may affect later preparation and assignments, making this more than a matter of wording. The case does not establish a complete causal chain or a particular remedy. Staff should be able to see what happened to their input without being portrayed as endorsing the version.

links.name: Answer 1
links.text: A. Announce that the new staff approved the finished version.

links.name: Answer 2
links.text: B. Explain what can happen next, preserve the concern, and connect it to an appropriate future opening without promising a change.

links.name: Answer 3
links.text: C. Discard the concern because it arrived after this version closed.

slides.text:
Consider the possible effects
Offering a concern is not approval. Repeated endorsement claims can suppress candid workplace input. Preserve the missing-route question and describe its actual next opening; staff agreement and a revised result are unknown.

How would you value the concern without claiming influence it cannot yet have?
Try another response
Continue learning
slides.narration: The new staff supplied a concern about a missing route, not an endorsement of the document. Turning their participation into approval can make later feedback less candid. Keep the account’s meaning and explain what remains possible. Repeated barriers in onboarding may affect development, but this case does not establish those effects or show that the staff agree with the finished version.

slides.text:
Why this response helps
This gives the concern a truthful route into later work. Repeated unavailable question routes can limit preparation through the life cycle. Explain the opening and actual responsibility; a future change and its effects are not yet established.

How would you value the concern without claiming influence it cannot yet have?
Continue learning
Try another response
slides.narration: The response recognizes the real limit and keeps the useful question alive. It connects input to an opening that can actually be considered through existing responsibilities. That is more credible than promising an immediate change or treating a concern as agreement. A later revision may address the route, but the effect on preparation and opportunity needs examination in actual use.

slides.text:
Consider the possible effects
The closed version limits immediate influence, not the value of the knowledge. Discarding repeated accounts may preserve the same onboarding gate. Explain a real next opening and consider the concern there; the appropriate remedy remains open.

How would you value the concern without claiming influence it cannot yet have?
Try another response
Continue learning
slides.narration: Timing affects what can change now, but it does not make the experience irrelevant. If late accounts are always discarded, the organization may repeatedly reproduce a condition that new employees are uniquely able to notice. A better response preserves the concern and explains an appropriate next opening. Do not invent a promised revision, timeline, or authority simply to make the answer reassuring.

slides.text:
Workplace participation has related limits
New employees may be invited to comment on onboarding after the next version is already final. Their experience is heard but cannot affect that version.

Explain the next genuine opening. Repeated invitations without an influence route can restrict whose knowledge shapes later learning and development.
slides.narration: Employee input is not community partnership, but a related influence question applies. Someone may have useful knowledge about how onboarding worked and still have no way to connect it with a change. Follow the account from recruitment through onboarding and development where relevant. The response should explain whether this concern can influence the current version, a later revision, or another appropriate inquiry. That clarity values the contribution without suggesting that a listening conversation has changed a document or created decision authority.

slides.text:
Culture briefs help prepare, not predict
Use a brief to consider questions about trust, meaning, or communication. Ask participants what matters to this decision.

A person’s identity does not assign a viewpoint or a representative role. Leave room for different experiences within every community.
slides.narration: A brief can help staff recognize questions they might otherwise overlook. It cannot tell them whether a participant wants a particular service option or what an entire community considers respectful. Keep the preparation separate from the person’s account. Invite an explanation without requiring a personal story or identity disclosure. That approach allows cultural understanding to deepen the conversation while preserving the participant’s authorship of their meaning and the range of perspectives that a real partnership may contain.

slides.text:
An account is not automatic endorsement
A contribution may ask a question, identify a concern, or offer an alternative. Record what it actually does.

Participation does not establish agreement with the proposal or permission to publish a personal story. Clarify use and attribution through the actual arrangements.
slides.narration: A person who improves a sentence may still disagree with the service approach. Someone who joins a discussion may not want their account shared publicly. These distinctions matter because a summary can give the organization apparent endorsement that was never offered. Repeating that practice may discourage candor in later exchanges. A careful account states what the person contributed, how it informed the work, and what remains unresolved. Permission and actual information responsibilities should be addressed rather than assumed.

slides.text:
Keep disagreement informative
Compare the reasons behind different views against the same decision question. Do not force several concerns into one community position.

A disagreement may reveal a tradeoff or a missing condition. Explain how the alternatives were considered without claiming unanimous approval.
slides.narration: Suppose one participant values an immediate answer and another values preparation before discussing an option. The perspectives may point toward more than one usable route. They do not establish a division between rigid community types. Ask what each account means for the actual task and compare the alternatives fairly. A decision can retain disagreement and still have a reasoned basis. The return should show that the concerns were considered without describing an unresolved preference as a shared endorsement.

slides.text:
From an account to an open question
A participant says the service notice leaves no usable way to clarify a next step. Connect that concern to the route being examined.

Avoid reducing it to a quotation on a welcome page. Knowledge becomes influential when its meaning informs a question or alternative that can still change.
slides.narration: A quotation can demonstrate that someone spoke without showing how their knowledge affected the work. Follow the contribution into the actual question. In this example, the concern may justify comparing contact routes or revising the explanation of available help. The alternative still needs examination, and the participant has not necessarily endorsed it. This connection makes engagement more substantive: the account shapes what staff consider rather than serving mainly as evidence that a meeting occurred.

slides.text:
A quotation in the summary
A participant asks for a usable way to clarify a service notice. Staff publish the quotation as evidence of community support, without examining the route or confirming public use. What is a better response?
A. Keep the summary because the quotation is positive about participation.
B. Use a culture brief to infer the participant’s preferred route.
C. Clarify use of the account, preserve its concern, and examine an open contact-route question through the appropriate responsibilities.
In Slide Show view, select a response to explore its effects.
slides.narration: This account offers a practical concern that can inform the service inquiry. Publishing it as support changes its meaning and may also use it beyond what the person expected. The stronger response clarifies the actual use and attribution arrangements, then follows the concern into a question that can still change. A culture brief can prepare respectful inquiry, but it cannot choose a route for the participant. Repeated treatment of accounts as publicity can leave the same service barriers untouched. Neither participation nor a published quotation establishes endorsement or improved understanding of the service.

links.name: Answer 1
links.text: A. Keep the summary because the quotation is positive about participation.

links.name: Answer 2
links.text: B. Use a culture brief to infer the participant’s preferred route.

links.name: Answer 3
links.text: C. Clarify use of the account, preserve its concern, and examine an open contact-route question through the appropriate responsibilities.

slides.text:
Consider the possible effects
Participation is not endorsement, and the concern remains unanswered. Repeated use as publicity can detach knowledge from decisions. Clarify permission and examine the route; support for the service has not been established.

What should the participant recognize in the account of how their input was used?
Try another response
Continue learning
slides.narration: A quotation can show that someone contributed without showing support for the proposal. Using it that way may discourage people from sharing concerns next time, while the missing route remains. Preserve the actual request and clarify permission for public use through the appropriate arrangements. The participant’s view of the whole service and the practical route they prefer are not supplied.

slides.text:
Consider the possible effects
The brief cannot select this person’s preference. Repeating that inference can replace their knowledge with a group assumption. Ask about the actual concern and usable routes; preference and practical feasibility remain open.

What should the participant recognize in the account of how their input was used?
Try another response
Continue learning
slides.narration: A brief helps prepare questions; it is not an answer from this person. Using it to infer a route may overlook their actual need and reproduce the same assumption in later design decisions. Ask what makes clarification usable and compare practical alternatives. The person does not need to represent a whole community, and the case supplies no confirmed preference or permission for public attribution.

slides.text:
Why this response helps
This connects the account with a genuine question and respects its use. Repeated missing routes can restrict service understanding. Examine alternatives and explain consideration; permission, agreement, and a better result cannot be assumed.

What should the participant recognize in the account of how their input was used?
Continue learning
Try another response
slides.narration: This response restores the account as knowledge that can inform the work. It respects the person’s control over how their contribution is described while retaining actual agency responsibilities. Examining the route may address a recurring barrier, but a proposed alternative is not yet an observed result. Explain what was considered and leave agreement, permission, and effectiveness open until established.

slides.text:
Return reasons, including limits
Explain which contributions informed the change, which did not, and why. Name what is still under consideration through the appropriate route.

A truthful return may include disagreement. It should not expose private details or promise influence over a decision outside the exchange.
slides.narration: People can understand that every suggestion will not be adopted when they can see a fair account of consideration. The explanation should connect the concern with the reasoned response and acknowledge limits. It might describe a revised contact route while naming an unresolved resource question. That return is different from a general thank-you. Repeatedly making the use of input understandable can support a more credible relationship, although trust itself should not be declared as an achieved outcome without people’s experience.

slides.text:
Rewrite the invitation
Choose one question that remains open. State what people can examine, what information is available, and how their contribution will be considered.

Remove a claim that participation means endorsement. What practical question would you want answered before deciding whether to contribute?
slides.narration: Try drafting the invitation as if you were deciding whether it deserved your own time. You would want a clear purpose, an honest account of influence, and enough information to understand the effort. The reflection does not require a new project or a prescribed meeting format. It helps you identify which part of an existing invitation is vague or misleading. A precise question can create room for substantive input while respecting actual decisions, practical limits, and the person’s freedom to decline.

slides.text:
Examine influence and experience separately
A draft change can show how a contribution influenced the work. A participant’s account can describe how the exchange felt and worked.

Neither automatically establishes broad trust or lasting service improvement. Examine the intended results through evidence suited to each question.
slides.narration: A comparison of draft versions may show that a concern changed the proposed route. That is meaningful evidence about influence. It does not establish that every participant found the process respectful or that the eventual service worked better. Ask those questions separately through usable and appropriate methods. Keeping the distinctions visible makes the assessment more informative. It also prevents a successful document change from hiding a participation barrier that remains for the next decision.

slides.text:
Sustain the relationship without making demands
Make the next genuine opening understandable and preserve the option not to participate. Do not assume a previous contribution commits someone to future work.

A continuing relationship can carry knowledge forward without turning one person into the permanent voice of a community.
slides.narration: Continuity can help people understand the work and help staff learn from experience over time. Yet a previous contribution is not a standing obligation. Ask what future participation would involve and recognize that interests or capacity may change. Broaden the inquiry where needed rather than repeatedly relying on the same person to represent everyone. The sustained practice is an honest relationship around actual choices, not a demand for constant availability or an assumption that familiarity establishes universal representation.

slides.text:
A partnership people can understand
Connect open choices, usable participation, and a clear return about influence. Preserve different accounts and actual responsibilities.

Community knowledge can reshape a question and improve an alternative. Its contribution should remain visible without overstating agreement, representation, or results.
slides.narration: You have examined partnership through what people can influence and how their knowledge reaches the work. A warm invitation matters, but its practical meaning depends on the open question and the conditions for contribution. Consider an exchange in your own work and ask where a participant’s account could change the inquiry. Making that connection clearer can support a useful relationship while keeping authority, resources, privacy, and unresolved choices honest. That is a meaningful foundation for continuing community-informed practice.

outcomes: Identify which choices remain open and which actual responsibilities remain fixed.
Compare participation designs for access, influence, and burden.
Explain how expertise, support, and compensation questions affect participation.
Prepare a truthful account of how input will be considered and returned.
